Parnell's mustached bat, Pteronotus parnellii, exhibits a life history shaped by the stable thermal conditions of its neotropical cave roosts. Basal metabolic rate, measured under standard conditions at a body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], reaches a peak of 30.70 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 30.70 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that reflects the high energetic demands of sustained echolocation and flight in a relatively small-bodied insectivore. This resting metabolic rate is considerably elevated compared to other bats of similar mass, likely due to the species' reliance on constant, high-frequency calls for prey detection in cluttered forest environments. Neonates enter the world weighing a mere 4 grams [Wwb = 4 grams] at parturition, a birth mass estimated from comparative data on the congeneric Pteronotus davyi. This altricial newborn is entirely dependent on maternal care, and its low mass relative to the adult female underscores the significant energetic investment required during gestation and subsequent lactation.

Female Pteronotus parnellii attain an ultimate wet weight for females of 16 grams [Wwi = 16 grams], a figure representing the upper end of the reported mass range for reproductively mature individuals in this species. This adult body mass is achieved after a period of sustained growth post-weaning and is a critical determinant of reproductive success, as larger females are often capable of producing healthier offspring. The species produces a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter] and, under the typical cave microclimate at a body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], females give birth to just one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year]. This low maximum reproductive output is a classic correlate of a K-selected life history strategy, where parental investment per offspring is prioritized over high fecundity, a pattern common among long-lived, tropical bat species.

The gestation period for Pteronotus parnellii spans 85 days [tg = 85 days] when the mother maintains a body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], a duration that is prolonged relative to many other insectivorous bats of comparable size. This extended gestation time may be linked to the energetic constraints imposed by a diet of flying insects, which can be seasonally variable, and the need for the developing foetus to reach a sufficient size for a successful live birth. Following parturition, the altricial neonate undergoes a period of rapid development while nursing. The time since birth at weaning is 45.5 days [tx = 45.5 days], also recorded at a stable body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. This weaning age marks the point at which the juvenile bat becomes nutritionally independent from its mother, transitioning to a diet of self-caught prey.

This thermally dependent developmental trajectory means that young bats born late in the season or facing poor foraging conditions may experience delayed puberty. The onset of gonadal activity is thus not strictly age-driven but is modulated by the animal's ability to sustain a high metabolic rate. This long pre-reproductive period allows for the full development of the sophisticated echolocation system and flight musculature required for successful hunting.
